quotes.label: The mountain overlook
quotes.quote: After being rejected by the cottagers, the Monster confronts Frankenstein atop a snowy mountain.The Monster laments to Frankenstein about how he has been cast out of society and by his own creator. Nietzsche describes Unity as the belief in the "presence of an All which is infinitely superior" to humans, reflecting that people derive meaning from an all-encompassing world order (Nietzsche 17). He also states that as a man loses his faith in Unity, he "loses the belief in his own worth when no infinitely precious entity manifests itself through him," suggesting that individuals often derive their self-worth from believing that they are part of a greater order, so when that order cannot explain their suffering, they lose faith in such an order existing (Nietzsche 17).
quotes.analysis: The Monster's inability to explain why Frankenstein and Humanity rejects him despite his expectation of an ordered world reveals his weakening faith in Unity, moving him closer to psychological nihilism.

quotes.label: Frankenstein himself
quotes.quote: Though angry at Frankenstein, the Monster initially addresses him as his "natural lord and king,"
quotes.analysis: demonstrating that the Monster believes that the creator and creation follow natural, ordered roles (Shelley 69).

quotes.label: A shadow between the two characters.
quotes.quote: This worldview is challenged as the Monster claims that he "ought to be [Frankenstein's] Adam, but [he] is rather the fallen angel" (Shelley 69).
quotes.analysis: The juxtaposition between how the Monster believes he should be treated and his rejection by Frankenstein creates his faltering belief in Unity. When he cannot understand his creator’s rejection of the ordered relationship he expected, the Monster starts doubting that a proper order exists at all. The use of biblical characters showcases how the Monster has taken this expected order as something divinely promised. However, when the biblical relationship does not manifest, the Monster loses faith in there being any divine order.

quotes.label: The valley in the distance.
quotes.quote: Beyond the breakdown of the creator relationship, the Monster describes seeing "bliss" everywhere, "from which [he] alone was irrevocably excluded" despite him being "benevolent and good" (Shelley 69).’
quotes.analysis: His exclusion from human society despite being good goes against his expectation that the world operates on some defined order that rewards goodness with kindness and acceptance. When he cannot explain his isolation with his actions, his belief in Unity weakens further.

quotes.label: The Monster’s clenched hand.
quotes.quote: Plunging further into anger, the Monster vows to “keep no terms with [his] enemies” despite trying to negotiate terms with Frankenstein (Shelley 69).
quotes.analysis: This transformation from seeking justice to rejecting it reveals how the Monster loses any hope for a relationship with Frankenstein, diminishing his faith in Unity. The Monster’s change from seeking acceptance to rejecting the human world demonstrates his declining faith in Unity, bringing him closer to psychological nihilism.
